title: CHAPTER NINE. On Sacred Scripture's parts
english:
CHAPTER NINE
On Sacred Scripture's parts

So far the affections of Sacred Scripture have been treated: the parts follow — namely the canonical books of the Old and New Testament, written and approved by men inspired and directed by God's Holy Spirit, for authentically declaring the whole will of God that pertains to religion.

They are called canonical as legitimate and regular from the canon of which king David ([[Psalm 19:8 >> Bible:Psalm 19:8]]) and the Apostle ([[Galatians 1:6 >> Bible:Galatians 1:6]]-[[Galatians 1:9 >> Bible:Galatians 1:9]]; [[Galatians 6:16 >> Bible:Galatians 6:16]]; [[Philippians 3:15 >> Bible:Philippians 3:15]]-[[Philippians 3:16 >> Bible:Philippians 3:16]]) make mention — books which by those men who were inspired and directed by the Holy Spirit were written or approved for this, that they might be a perpetual norm and measure of faith and life according to the state and condition of each Testament ([[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]-[[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]; [[2 Peter 1:20 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:20]]-[[2 Peter 1:21 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:21]]), and they are opposed to the Apocrypha, that is, to all those that do not rule and measure the Christian faith.

For certain Apocrypha are also joined to these in the Bibles — irregulars — which for the usefulness of reading, not for their certain divinity, were sometimes called deuterocanonical and Ecclesiastical by the ancients, and can be referred to Sacred Scripture's parts only improperly, of which below at Aph. 13, 14, and 15. Canonical books are also called books existing by confession, testamentary, and by St. Athanasius books received into the canon, as in the variant readings of H. Savile on the Life of St. Antony edited by Heschel. And there is a double criterion from which judgment is made concerning each sacred writing that it is canonical accurately and specially so called — internal and external.

title: Internal criterion of the thing: inspiration; prophetic holiness and infallibility in writing
english: The internal criterion is of the thing or of the sign. The criterion of the thing is God's immediate inspiration, calling, and instruction ([[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]; [[2 Peter 1:20 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:20]]; [[Luke 16:29 >> Bible:Luke 16:29]]; [[Ephesians 2:20 >> Bible:Ephesians 2:20]]; [[Hebrews 1:1 >> Bible:Hebrews 1:1]]; Galatians 1 and 11-12, 15-16; [[Romans 15:18 >> Bible:Romans 15:18]]) — of him who wrote the Scriptures with God inspiring, indeed by whose hands God himself wrote, as Alphonsus de Castro speaks, Against Heresies book 1 chapter 2 page 4.

From which we gather: (1) that the prophets or canonical writers have holiness in living ([[2 Peter 1:21 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:21]]) — not a holiness that means absolute impeccability ([[1 Kings 8:46 >> Bible:1 Kings 8:46]]; [[2 Chronicles 6:36 >> Bible:2 Chronicles 6:36]]; [[Ecclesiastes 7:21 >> Bible:Ecclesiastes 7:21]]; [[Proverbs 20:9 >> Bible:Proverbs 20:9]]), but one that excludes voluntary sins, malice, stubbornness, and an evil purpose — that is, sins against conscience ([[1 John 3 >> Bible:1 John 3]]).

(2) The same men's infallibility in writing, because he writes not as a man but as a holy man of God ([[2 Peter 1:21 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:21]]), led by the Spirit of truth into all truth ([[John 14:17 >> Bible:John 14:17]]; [[John 16:13 >> Bible:John 16:13]]; [[2 Peter 1:21 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:21]]) — by the example of converted David ([[Matthew 22:43 >> Bible:Matthew 22:43]]; [[Psalm 45:2 >> Bible:Psalm 45:2]]; [[2 Samuel 23:2 >> Bible:2 Samuel 23:2]]). For if error and falsehood were admitted into so high a summit of authority, no particle of these books would remain that could not be called into doubt, as Augustine well warns in Letter 8 to Jerome.

Therefore, that the Evangelists' writings may stand as canonical and authentic and their authority remain safe, every falsehood ought to be absent from them — not only what is put forward by lying, but also what comes by forgetting — as the same teaches in On the Harmony of the Gospels book 1 chapter 12. Yet judgment about the prophets' infallibility is to be made from the truth of God which they reveal dogmatically, not from the history of a deed and of a speech which they sometimes recount as in character, as [[Genesis 3:1 >> Bible:Genesis 3:1]], [[Genesis 3:4 >> Bible:Genesis 3:4]]-[[Genesis 3:5 >> Bible:Genesis 3:5]]; [[John 8:44 >> Bible:John 8:44]] — according to Ruiz's rule 219: an evangelical narrative, though most true, yet not all things said there are believed to be true, from Augustine, Against the Priscillianists chapter 9.

title: Prophetic divinity; criterion of the sign (Hebrew and Greek); external catholic testimony
english: (3) The divinity, majesty, sharpness, and wonderful force and efficacy of prophecy ([[Hebrews 4:12 >> Bible:Hebrews 4:12]]; [[James 1:21 >> Bible:James 1:21]]; [[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]; [[Romans 1:16 >> Bible:Romans 1:16]]; [[Luke 24:32 >> Bible:Luke 24:32]]; [[John 6:68 >> Bible:John 6:68]]) — which even Stenius from the papal flock acknowledges in the opening of his Cosmopoeia.

The criterion of the sign is one thing for the Old Testament, another for the New. The Old Testament's is the Hebrew tongue, by Justin's witness in Apology 2 for the Christians — except a few pericopes in Daniel, Ezra, and Jeremiah written in the Chaldean idiom. Whether Arabic and Syriac words are sometimes mixed into Job — to say nothing of Greek words — is a deeper inquiry; on which see M. Mayer's Sacred Philology page 151. The New Testament's is the Greek tongue, in which the whole is written — though Baronius, Annals volume 1 at year 45, holds that Mark wrote not in Greek but in Latin, and wins assent from Kirsten in the preface to his Arabic Grammar page 36; and concerning Matthew's Gospel the matter is more tangled — consult Flacius Illyricus in the preface to the Gloss on Matthew, Isaac Casaubon Exercises 15 chapter 1 page 279 and 16 chapter 15 page 485, Johannes Drusius Observations on the New Testament chapter 1, and others.

But the external criterion is the catholic testimony of the primitive and true church concerning each Testament's autograph — from which, in the time of Ezra and Malachi, the Old Testament canon was constituted, and the New's in the time of the Apostolic men and was finished by John the Apocalyptist. For that reason, if there are any sacred books that lack testimony from the autograph and against which the church that flourished when the canon was set has catholically contradicted, they are not trustworthy.

title: Inferences 1-2: canonical authority for each listed book; one unchanging canon reason
english: From which we conclude: (1) That canonical authority belongs to each of the Old and New Testament books enumerated by us below — from Moses to Malachi and from Matthew to the Apocalypse.

(2) That the Old and New canons' reason is one and the same, which no antiquity obliterates and no novelty varies. Hence the papal distinction between a Hebrew and a Christian canon as to the Old Testament is null — as is also the doubling of the Hebrew canon so that one would be of the Hebrew prophets and another of the Seventy interpreters, which Genebrard has in the preface of Chronology to Arnold Pontanus.

Stapleton also errs, Principles of Doctrine book 9 chapter 6, asserting that certain non-canonical books can become canonical — namely those written in the Apostles' time. And Tanner, Disputation 1 on Thomas part 1, Disputation 5 on the written and unwritten word, thesis 37: "It is not," he says, "altogether improbable what some say, that the Church can even now receive some book newly into the canon." Whom Bellarmine rightly contradicts, On the Word of God book 1 chapter 10: "We confess," he says, "that the church can IN NO WAY make a non-canonical book canonical: but only declare which is to be held for canonical."

title: Inferences 3-4: canons judge controversies; adequate sufficiency against unwritten word
english: (3) That all canonical books can judge and determine controversies of religion. For this is the canon's force ([[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]-[[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]; [[Psalm 119:9 >> Bible:Psalm 119:9]]; [[Romans 2:16 >> Bible:Romans 2:16]]; [[Hebrews 4:12 >> Bible:Hebrews 4:12]]; [[John 3:18 >> Bible:John 3:18]]; [[John 12:48 >> Bible:John 12:48]]; [[John 16:8 >> Bible:John 16:8]]). And Sacred Scripture judges and determines as a rule, with the Holy Spirit speaking through it president in it — this one or that with his assessors — by way of the person to whom it falls; who if he is an uncorrupted judge, the judgment of all these becomes one and the same, and so divine and infallible — on which Cornelius Martinius among our philosophers teaches more rightly in Analysis part 2 chapter 3 than Bellarmine in On the Word of God book 3 chapter 9.

(4) The sacred canon's self-sufficiency and its adequate sufficiency for Christian faith and manners — by which all things necessary for Christians to believe and do are contained in it in due manner — so that today, after God's word has been committed to letters and entrusted to the Church, we are in no way bound to receive with equal pious affection, together with the written word of God, another unwritten word of God, or one not written in the Bibles but handed down from the Apostles in Cabbalah-fashion, as necessary for salvation and for establishing other dogmas of faith that stand in the Bibles neither as to letter nor as to sense. For both the name "canon" by which Scripture is marked ([[Psalm 19:5 >> Bible:Psalm 19:5]]; [[Galatians 6:16 >> Bible:Galatians 6:16]]) and the thing itself teach this ([[Psalm 19:8 >> Bible:Psalm 19:8]]; [[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]-[[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]; [[James 1:21 >> Bible:James 1:21]]; [[John 20:31 >> Bible:John 20:31]]; [[John 5:39 >> Bible:John 5:39]]; [[1 Corinthians 4:6 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 4:6]]; [[Galatians 1:8 >> Bible:Galatians 1:8]]).

Against the sophistic charge of imperfection from John Fisher Bishop of Rochester, John Eck, Conrad Kling, Wilhelm Lindanus, Melchior Cano, Martin Perez de Ayala, Rene Benoist, Alphonsus de Castro, Franz Agricola, Gregory of Valencia, Robert Bellarmine, Francis Coster, Thomas Stapleton, Heinrich Lancellot, Vitus Miletus, Adam Tanner, James Gordon Huntly, and Martin Becanus — against which false prophets and their whole papal examination read the most learned Dr. Antonius Thysius, Leiden theologian, succinctly and learnedly treating of canonical and Apocryphal books in Synopsis of Purer Theology Disputation 3, with others praised there by us.

title: Aph. II-IV: Old Testament canonical books; historical, poetic, prophetic; Pentateuch, Triteuch, Octateuch
english: II. The canonical books of the Old Testament are no others than those of which it is catholically established that they were written in Hebrew and partly in Chaldean, and were acknowledged as divine by the ancient Jewish Church.
III. The canonical books of the Old Testament are partly historical, partly poetic, partly prophetic.

IV. The historical are the Pentateuch, the Triteuch, and the Octateuch. The word Pentateuch is commonly known; Triteuch stands in Athanasius's Letter to Marcellinus page 581; Octateuch in Procopius of Gaza the sophist's commentary on the eight books of the Old Testament.

title: Aph. V-VIII: contents of Pentateuch, Triteuch, Octateuch; poetic books
english: V. The Pentateuch contains Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy — see Contracted Theology, Book 1, Chapter 9, Aphorisms 6-10.
VI. The Triteuch embraces three books, namely Joshua, Judges, and Ruth. See Aphorisms 11-13.

VII. The Octateuch is that which contains the eight following books: the two of Samuel, the two of Kings, the two of Chronicles, the book of Ezra and Nehemiah, and the book of Esther. See there Aph. 14-15 and following through 23.

VIII. And these are the historical books of the ancient Hebrew canon. The poetic follow, which are the most elegant practice and epitome of the law and the prophets — as Job, the Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs. See Chapter 11 on the poetic books.

title: Aph. IX-XII: prophetic books; major and minor prophets
english: IX. The prophetic books are those that, besides manifold predictions, comprise an accurate interpretation of the Mosaic law, a prudent and exact application of moral doctrine, of divine promises and threatenings — especially of the gracious covenant whose foundation is Christ — and the true use of the divine law.
X. And some are major, others minor.
XI. The major are Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel. See Chapter 12 on the prophetic books.

XII. The minor are twelve, who comprised their sermons in shorter booklets than those: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. On which see Sirach 49:11 and our Chapter 13 on the twelve prophets.

title: Aph. XIII-XV: Apocrypha defined; historical and didactic Apocrypha
english: XIII. These are the canonical books of the Old Testament, to which the Apocrypha are commonly added — not on equal thread — books written indeed by pious and skilled authors, of which it is not yet catholically established whether they were inspired by the Holy Spirit and directed to this, that by them they should enlarge the canon of faith and life; finally inserted among the canonical books for the usefulness of reading. Apocrypha are here so called from a hidden disclosure; they are opposed to the testamentary books — Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith book 4 chapter 18. And since the history and reason of this first name's imposition almost escapes us, we judge it safest that the Apocrypha be described from opposition to the canonicals — seeing they are not equal to them in thread.

XIV. These are partly historical, partly didactic. The historical are the book of Tobit, the Prayer of Manasseh, the book of Judith, Baruch, the Letter of Jeremiah, the additions in Daniel, Ezra's third and fourth books, the additions to Esther, the book of Simon the high priest commonly called Third Maccabees, and First and Second Maccabees. See there chapter 14 on the Apocryphal books from the beginning through Aphorism 14.
XV. The didactic are the book of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus.

title: Aph. XVI-XVIII: New Testament canonical books; four integral parts; evangelical part
english: XVI. And thus far the Apocrypha also. There follow the canonical books of the New Testament, which are the tables of the most holy contract between God and the human race, established by the blood of the Lamb of God already slain — written by eight scribes, most excellent men, witnesses beyond all exception, inspired by the Holy Spirit.
XVII. And the integral parts of the New Testament are four: one Evangelical, another practical, a third epistolary, and finally a fourth Apocalyptic.

XVIII. The Evangelical part was written by the four Evangelists — Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John — concerning the conception, birth, teaching, life, wonderful works, passion, death, departure to the Father, and return of Jesus of Nazareth, with great agreement in the matter, to demonstrate that this one is the promised Messiah.

title: Aph. XIX-XXII: practical part (Acts); epistolary part; Paul's fourteen letters
english: XIX. The practical is the second part, written by Luke at Rome by the will of Paul the prisoner — concerning the birth and infancy, growth, and just, gracious, and most simple face, teaching, strength, and whole form of government of the optimally constituted primitive Church of Christ and of reunion, and concerning the deeds of the Apostles fighting against false doctrine, described under the face and condition of the Ephesian Church ([[Revelation 2:1 >> Bible:Revelation 2:1]]).

XX. The epistolary is the third part of the New Testament, written by the Apostles in epistolary character concerning the chief heads of Christian religion and the very practice of Christian faith and life in truth, according to the measure of each one's gift and calling, to be exercised by anyone in the course of this pilgrimage until the world's end — written to those absent from the Old Testament, Christ's sermons, and the Holy Spirit's suggestion.
XXI. The Apostolic epistles were written partly by Paul — namely fourteen — partly by James — namely one — partly by Peter — namely two — partly by John — namely three — partly by Jude — namely one.

XXII. Paul wrote these by name: one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, one to Philemon, one to the Hebrews.

title: Aph. XXIII: Apocalyptic part; Cap. 9 close
english: XXIII. There remains the Apocalyptic, the fourth part of the New Testament, written by the Apostle John concerning those things which Christ himself revealed about the state of the New Testament churches — from its beginning through seven distinct periods and faces portrayed in the Ephesian, Smyrnaean, Pergamene, Thyatiran, Sardian, Philadelphian, and Laodicean, unto the world's end — and concerning their gifts, dangers, calamities, Antichrist's persecutions, deliverances, the last judgment, the dreadful damnation of the impious, and the supreme glorification of the churches and the godly in it — lest, ignorant of their own fates and future lot, like Gentiles or brute beasts, they should be overwhelmed and perish by sudden chances; but taught little by little by the experience of predicted events, they might acknowledge that they are always Christ's care.
